analysis.one_liner: Bars police and intelligence agencies from buying Americans' personal data from brokers without a court order.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 219-199 on April 17, 2024, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop police and intelligence agencies from buying Americans' personal data — location, browsing history, communications records — from data brokers instead of getting a warrant. It would require a court order before the government could obtain such records from a third party, forbid agencies from sharing broker-bought data with each other or using it as evidence, and extend existing communications-privacy rules to the intermediary companies that store and transmit data behind the scenes. The House passed it 219-199, but the Senate never acted and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose location, browsing history, search history, and account records are currently collected and sold by data brokers. The bill would bar police and intelligence agencies from simply buying that data — including data obtained illegitimately — and would require them to get a court order under the toughest applicable standard instead. It would also extend existing wiretap-law privacy protections to the intermediary companies that store and transmit communications behind the scenes, and block data bought from brokers from being used as evidence in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with a phone or online account

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits law enforcement agencies and intelligence agencies from obtaining covered records — communications, location data, and account records — or illegitimately obtained information from a third party in exchange for anything of value, closing the practice of buying data that would otherwise require a court order.

Requires the government to get a court order before acquiring such records from a third party, with courts applying the most stringent standard that federal statute or the Constitution would require for a comparable demand on a phone or internet provider.

Bars other government agencies from sharing broker-purchased records with law enforcement and intelligence agencies, and bars the use of records obtained in violation of the ban — and any evidence derived from them — in any trial, hearing, or proceeding.

Extends the Stored Communications Act's ban on divulging communications contents and customer records to intermediary service providers — the companies that deliver, store, or process communications behind the scenes for phone and internet providers.

Makes the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act the exclusive legal means for acquiring Americans' location information, web browsing history, search history, and communications records for foreign intelligence purposes, rather than leaving those acquisitions to informal agency purchases.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers lose a lucrative line of business: selling Americans' location, browsing, and account records to police and intelligence agencies, and reselling data scraped or bought in violation of companies' own terms. Law enforcement and intelligence agencies lose a warrant-free shortcut to this data, and technology companies that store or transmit communications on behalf of phone and internet providers take on new legal restrictions on what they can hand over.

drawbacks.text: The protections have carve-outs: data voluntarily made public, public government records, and data generated by automated license plate reader systems are all excluded, and background-check uses with written consent are allowed.

The definition of 'illegitimately obtained information' leans heavily on private companies' own service agreements and privacy policies, so the scope of protection depends on the contract language individual providers happen to write.

The bill removes a data channel agencies currently use without warrants, which could slow or block some investigations that fall short of the standard needed for a court order; a bipartisan bloc found this unacceptable, with 109 of 216 House Democrats voting no.

Restricting what intermediary providers may disclose shifts compliance decisions onto private companies that store and transmit other firms' communications, a duty they did not previously carry under the wiretap statutes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to everyone: a warrant requirement for data the government currently buys off the shelf, and a ban on using broker-purchased data as evidence. The costs are real but narrower — some investigations will face friction, and the data-broker industry loses a revenue stream. The bill is not airtight: the license-plate-reader and public-data carve-outs and the reliance on private contracts to define 'illegitimate' leave meaningful gaps. Still, the protection it would have added was broad, and the reason it did not become law was not a floor vote against it but the Senate declining to act at all.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 219-199, but after the Senate received it on April 18, 2024, nobody ever brought it to a vote, and it died when the term ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced July 14, 2023, and referred to the Judiciary and Intelligence committees.
The Judiciary Committee ordered it reported by a unanimous 30-0 vote on July 19, 2023, and formally reported it on April 15, 2024; the Intelligence Committee was discharged the same day.
The House passed it on April 17, 2024, by a vote of 219-199 with 1 voting present — Democrats 96-109 in favor, Republicans 123-90.
The Senate received the bill on April 18, 2024, and took no further action; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers keep their government sales, and agencies keep the ability to buy Americans' location, browsing, and account data from third parties without a court order. Everyone whose data is being sold continues to have no protection against the practice.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and agencies buying data

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 14, 2023, steered it through committee, and managed it on the House floor, including moving that the Committee of the Whole rise to advance it.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported by a unanimous 30-0 committee vote on July 19, 2023, and reported it with H. Rept. 118-459 in April 2024.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported a rule (H. Res. 1149) on April 16, 2024 that put H.R. 4639 on the floor under a structured rule with one hour of debate and one motion to recommit.

for.name: Civil liberties groups such as the ACLU and EFF
for.what_they_did: Supported the civil liberties coalition behind the bill, which framed it as closing the loophole allowing police to buy data they would need a warrant to obtain.

against.name: 109 of 216 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage of the bill, 109-96 within the caucus.

against.name: 90 of 224 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage of the bill, 90-123 within the caucus.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote after it arrived from the House on April 18, 2024; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Intelligence and law enforcement agencies
against.role: FBI, DHS, and other agencies purchasing broker data
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative restrictions on their ability to buy commercially available location and personal data without a court order, an authority they had been using in investigations.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split both parties: House Democrats voted 96-109 in favor, Republicans 123-90, so the yes coalition was genuinely bipartisan and neither party was unified.

industries.note: The bill's core target: brokers that aggregate and resell Americans' location, browsing, and account data would lose the ability to sell it to law enforcement and intelligence agencies and to traffic in data obtained in violation of service agreements or by deception.

Agencies that currently buy commercially available data to avoid the warrant process would have to get court orders instead, could not share purchased data across agencies, and could not use illegally obtained broker data as evidence.

Companies that deliver, store, or process communications on behalf of phone and internet providers would face new prohibitions on divulging contents and customer records, adding compliance duties but giving them clear statutory privacy rules.

The ecosystem of apps and license-plate cameras feeding location and plate data to brokers keeps a carve-out: data from automated license plate reader systems is expressly excluded from the bill's protections, so that part of the surveillance-data market is untouched.
